title: The Molecules of Heredity
summary: Learn the chemical building blocks of DNA and RNA and how they are packaged inside cells.

lessons.title: Nucleotides: Bases, Sugars and Phosphates

levels.kid:
DNA is like a very long necklace. Each bead on the necklace is called a **nucleotide**.

Every bead has three parts glued together:
- A **sugar**, which is the middle of the bead.
- A **phosphate**, which is the hook that links one bead to the next.
- A **base**, which is like a letter.

DNA uses just four letters: A, G, C and T. With only four letters, your cells write instructions for making your eyes, your muscles and even your brain!

The sugars and phosphates link up to make a strong backbone, like the string of the necklace. The bases stick out to the side, so the cell can read them like words in a book.
levels.hs:
DNA and RNA are **nucleic acids**, long chains built from repeating units called **nucleotides**. Each nucleotide has three parts:
- A **nitrogenous base**: a ring-shaped molecule containing nitrogen.
- A **five-carbon sugar** (a pentose): **deoxyribose** in DNA, **ribose** in RNA.
- One or more **phosphate groups**.

The bases come in two families. **Purines** have two fused rings: **adenine (A)** and **guanine (G)**. **Pyrimidines** have a single ring: **cytosine (C)**, **thymine (T)** in DNA, and **uracil (U)** in RNA.

A base attached to a sugar, with no phosphate, is called a **nucleoside**. Add a phosphate and it becomes a nucleotide. To tell the sugar's carbons apart from the base's atoms, scientists number them with a "prime": 1′ through 5′. The base attaches at the 1′ carbon and the phosphate at the 5′ carbon.

Nucleotides join through **phosphodiester bonds**. The phosphate on one sugar's 5′ carbon links to the 3′ carbon of the next sugar. This builds a sugar-phosphate backbone with a direction: one end is the **5′ end** and the other is the **3′ end**.

A real example is **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate). It is a nucleotide with three phosphates, and it is the cell's main energy currency. Its cousin **dATP** is one of the building blocks used to make DNA.
levels.college:
**Structure of a nucleotide.** A nucleotide is a base joined to a pentose sugar, which carries one to three phosphates on its 5′ carbon.
- The base attaches to the C1′ carbon through an **N-glycosidic bond**. Purines bond through N9 and pyrimidines through N1.
- In DNA, **2′-deoxyribose** has a hydrogen at C2′. In RNA, ribose has a 2′-OH.
- The phosphates are named α, β and γ, starting from the one closest to the sugar.

**Naming.**
- Nucleosides: adenosine, guanosine, cytidine, uridine, and (deoxy)thymidine.
- Nucleotides: AMP, ADP and ATP, and their deoxy forms (dAMP, dATP and so on).

**Bases.** Purines (A, G) are bicyclic, made of a pyrimidine ring fused to an imidazole ring. Pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one six-membered ring. Thymine is simply 5-methyluracil. Bases are flat and aromatic, so they absorb UV light strongly near **260 nm**. This is the basis of measuring DNA concentration by spectrophotometry.

**Polymerization.** Polymerases add a **deoxynucleoside triphosphate (dNTP)** to the 3′-OH of a growing chain. The 3′-OH attacks the α-phosphate, which releases **pyrophosphate (PPi)**. Cellular pyrophosphatases then hydrolyze PPi into two phosphates, which pulls the reaction forward. The result is a 3′→5′ phosphodiester linkage, and chains grow 5′→3′.

**Charge.** Each phosphodiester carries one negative charge at physiological pH (its pKa is about 1). This makes nucleic acids polyanions. They bind Mg²⁺, histone lysines and arginines, and they move toward the positive electrode in gel electrophoresis.

**Sugar pucker.** The furanose ring is not flat. DNA nucleotides favor a **C2′-endo** pucker, and ribonucleotides favor **C3′-endo**. This small conformational difference affects the overall helix shape.
levels.phd:
**Biosynthesis.** Purines are built **on** the ribose: starting from PRPP, ten steps assemble the ring to make IMP, which then branches into AMP and GMP. Pyrimidines are built **first** as a free ring (orotate) and then attached to PRPP to make UMP. CTP synthetase aminates UTP to make CTP. Deoxyribonucleotides come from **ribonucleotide reductase (RNR)**, which reduces NDPs to dNDPs using a radical mechanism (a tyrosyl radical in class I RNR). RNR is allosterically controlled at an activity site (ATP activates, dATP inhibits) and a specificity site, which keeps the four dNTP pools balanced. Thymidylate is made by **thymidylate synthase**, which methylates dUMP using methylene-tetrahydrofolate. This step is a classic drug target for fluorouracil and, indirectly, methotrexate.

**Glycosidic conformation.** Rotation about the N-glycosidic bond (angle χ) gives **anti** or **syn** conformers. Pyrimidines are almost always anti because O2 clashes with the sugar in syn. Purines can adopt syn, and guanosine does so in Z-DNA.

**Tautomers.** Bases exist mainly in amino and keto forms. Watson and Crick's model succeeded partly because Jerry Donohue corrected the enol forms printed in textbooks of the time. Rare imino and enol tautomers were proposed early on as a source of mispairing and mutation. Modern NMR work (Al-Hashimi and colleagues) has detected transient, tautomeric and anionic Watson-Crick-like mismatches that polymerases can accept.

**Why phosphate?** Westheimer argued (1987) that phosphate suits the genome's backbone because its diester keeps a negative charge. This charge repels nucleophiles and slows hydrolysis, giving an uncatalysed half-life of millions of years at neutral pH, while still allowing enzymes to break the bond. The 2′-OH of RNA undoes much of this stability by attacking in-line to give a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate.

**Chemical fragility.** Even in DNA, the N-glycosidic bond hydrolyzes spontaneously, purines faster than pyrimidines (thousands of depurinations per cell per day). Cytosine also deaminates to uracil, which may help explain why DNA uses thymine.
levels.expert:
**Nucleotide analogues as drugs.** Much of antiviral and anticancer pharmacology exploits the nucleotide scaffold.
- **Chain terminators** lack a 3′-OH: azidothymidine (AZT) in HIV, and acyclovir, which herpes thymidine kinase selectively phosphorylates. Because the 3′-OH is the nucleophile, removing it stops chain extension.
- **Delayed or non-obligate terminators** keep the 3′-OH. Remdesivir stalls SARS-CoV-2 RdRp a few nucleotides downstream. Sofosbuvir (a 2′-fluoro-2′-C-methyluridine prodrug) blocks HCV NS5B.
- **Lethal mutagenesis**: molnupiravir's N4-hydroxycytidine switches between tautomers, pairing with either G or A, which piles up errors across the viral genome.

A recurring practical pitfall is the **first phosphorylation**. Cellular kinases often handle analogues poorly. ProTide chemistry (McGuigan) delivers a masked monophosphate to bypass this step.

**Nucleobase metabolism in the clinic.** Thiopurines (azathioprine, mercaptopurine) depend on TPMT and NUDT15 variants, and patients are genotyped before therapy. Fluoropyrimidine toxicity tracks **DPYD** variants, and guidelines now recommend pre-treatment testing. Methotrexate and pemetrexed starve cells of thymidylate and purines through folate pathways. Neuro-oncology relevance: temozolomide alkylates guanine at O6, and tumours silencing **MGMT** by promoter methylation respond better.

**Expanding the alphabet.** Romesberg's dNaM–dTPT3 hydrophobic pair works without hydrogen bonds and has been replicated in living *E. coli*. Benner's "hachimoji" system (2019) uses eight letters. These studies show that shape complementarity and stacking, not just H-bonding, can carry information.

**Research tools.** Fluorescent and modified nucleotides (dye-labelled reversible terminators in Illumina sequencing, EdU for click-chemistry detection of proliferating cells, biotin-dUTP) all depend on polymerases tolerating changes at C5 of pyrimidines or C7 of 7-deazapurines, which point into the major groove.

**Open questions:** how dNTP pool imbalance (SAMHD1 loss, RNR dysregulation) drives mutational signatures in tumours, and why prebiotic chemistry settled on ribose and these four bases.

The RNA-specific roles of these chemical features are covered in a later lesson.

keyPoints: A nucleotide = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + 1-3 phosphates
Purines (A, G) have two rings; pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one
DNA uses 2′-deoxyribose; RNA uses ribose with a 2′-OH
Nucleoside = base + sugar; adding phosphate makes a nucleotide
Phosphodiester bonds link 3′-OH to 5′-phosphate, giving 5′→3′ direction
Polymerases add dNTPs to the 3′-OH and release pyrophosphate

lessons.title: The Double Helix: Base Pairing, Grooves and Forms

levels.kid:
Imagine a twisty ladder, like a spiral staircase. That is what DNA looks like! Scientists call it a **double helix**.

The two side rails are made of sugar and phosphate. The steps in the middle are made of pairs of letters: A, T, G and C.

The letters have best friends. **A always holds hands with T**, and **G holds hands with C**. So if you know one side of the ladder, you can figure out the other side, like a puzzle with matching pieces.

Because the ladder twists, it has a wide gap and a narrow gap along its side. Special helper proteins slide into the gaps to read the letters without opening the ladder.
levels.hs:
DNA is a **double helix**: two strands wound around each other like a twisted ladder. James Watson and Francis Crick proposed this model in 1953, using X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling.

Key features:
- The **backbone** of each strand is alternating sugar and phosphate, on the outside of the helix.
- The **bases** point inward and pair up: adenine (A) with thymine (T), and guanine (G) with cytosine (C). These are **complementary base pairs**, held together by **hydrogen bonds**: two in an A-T pair, three in a G-C pair.
- The two strands run in opposite directions, which is called **antiparallel**. One runs 5' to 3', and its partner runs 3' to 5'.
- Because of how the sugars attach to the bases, the twist leaves two uneven grooves: a wide **major groove** and a narrow **minor groove**.

Example: if one strand reads 5'-ATGC-3', its partner reads 3'-TACG-5'.

Base pairing explains **Chargaff's rules**: in double-stranded DNA, the amount of A equals T, and G equals C. It also explains how DNA can be copied. Each strand is a template for building its partner.
levels.college:
The Watson-Crick double helix is two antiparallel polynucleotide strands coiled around a common axis.

**Base pairing.** A purine always faces a pyrimidine, so every pair has nearly the same width (about 1.08 nm between C1' atoms). This keeps the helix diameter steady at about 2 nm.
- A·T pairs share 2 hydrogen bonds.
- G·C pairs share 3 hydrogen bonds.

**What holds the helix together.** Helix stability comes mostly from **base stacking**, not hydrogen bonds. Stacking means van der Waals and hydrophobic contacts between neighbouring flat base pairs. Hydrogen bonds mainly supply **specificity**, meaning they decide which bases pair.

Because stacking energies vary with sequence, GC-rich DNA has a higher **melting temperature (Tm)**. Melting means the strands separate. Positive ions such as Na+ and Mg2+ shield the negatively charged phosphates and also raise Tm.

**Grooves.** The glycosidic bonds of a base pair sit on the same side of the pair, not directly opposite each other. This makes the two grooves unequal in size.
- In the major groove, each base pair displays a distinct pattern of hydrogen-bond donors, acceptors and methyl groups. Proteins can read this pattern without unwinding the DNA.
- The minor groove is less informative, because A·T and T·A look similar there.

**Helical forms.**
- **B-DNA** is the main form in cells. It is right-handed, with about 10.5 bp per turn and a 3.4 Å rise per base pair.
- **A-DNA** forms under dehydration and in RNA duplexes. It is right-handed and wider, with about 11 bp per turn and a deep, narrow major groove.
- **Z-DNA** is left-handed, with about 12 bp per turn and a zigzag backbone. It favours alternating purine-pyrimidine repeats such as (CG)n.

Heating DNA unstacks the bases, which raises absorbance at 260 nm. This **hyperchromic effect** is the basis of melting curves.
levels.phd:
The structure came from converging lines of evidence:
- Franklin and Gosling's Photo 51 showed a helical cross pattern, with a 3.4 Å base-pair spacing and a 34 Å repeat.
- Chargaff measured equal base ratios.
- Jerry Donohue corrected the base structures to their keto tautomers, which made Watson-Crick pairing possible.
- Atomic-resolution confirmation came only in 1980, when Dickerson's group solved the crystal structure of the dodecamer CGCGAATTCGCG.
- That structure also revealed a narrowed minor groove at the A-tract, with a bound spine of hydration.

**Sugar pucker and form.** The pucker of the deoxyribose sugar largely determines the helical form.
- B-DNA adopts C2'-endo pucker.
- A-form adopts C3'-endo pucker. This shortens the distance between neighbouring phosphates and tilts the base pairs about 20°.
- The ribose 2'-OH in RNA favours C3'-endo, so RNA duplexes and DNA-RNA hybrids are A-like. This matters for RNase H recognition and for siRNA design.
- Z-DNA alternates syn guanosine with anti cytidine, which produces its dinucleotide zigzag repeat.

**Stability is nearest-neighbour dependent.** SantaLucia's unified parameters (1998) assign a ΔH and ΔS to each of the 10 possible stacked dinucleotide steps. These are the basis of primer Tm prediction. Overall stability tracks stacking more than hydrogen-bond count.

**Non-canonical pairing.** Hoogsteen pairs use the purine N7 edge, typically with the purine flipped to syn. They appear transiently in B-DNA, with populations around 1% and lifetimes of milliseconds (Al-Hashimi, 2011, by NMR relaxation dispersion). Hoogsteen pairing also underlies triplexes and G-quadruplexes.

**Groove readout.** Seeman, Rosenberg and Rich (1976) showed that the major groove uniquely encodes base identity. Two readout modes are now recognised:
- **Base readout**: direct hydrogen bonding to groove atoms.
- **Shape readout**: proteins sense sequence-dependent minor-groove width and the resulting electrostatic potential (Rohs, 2009).
- For example, Arg side chains insert into narrow A-tract minor grooves.

**Topology.** Linking number, twist and writhe (Lk = Tw + Wr) link the geometry of the double helix to supercoiling.
levels.expert:
Helix geometry is directly exploited in research and therapy.

**Minor-groove binders.** Several drugs and dyes read the minor groove:
- Distamycin and netropsin prefer AT-rich narrow grooves.
- The dyes Hoechst 33258 and DAPI use the same preference to stain nuclei.
- **Trabectedin** alkylates guanine N2 from the minor groove and interferes with transcription-coupled repair.
- Dervan's pyrrole-imidazole polyamides extended this into programmable sequence recognition, using paired-ring codes. However, getting them into cells and nuclei limited clinical translation.

**Intercalators.** Doxorubicin, actinomycin D and ethidium slide between stacked base pairs. This lengthens and unwinds the helix: ethidium unwinds it by about 26° per molecule. Unwinding is the basis of the classic topoisomerase and supercoil gel assays.

**A-form geometry in RNA medicine.**
- Antisense gapmers work because the DNA-RNA hybrid they form is A-like, and RNase H1 recognises that intermediate geometry.
- Locking sugars into C3'-endo (LNA, 2'-O-methyl, 2'-F) raises affinity for the target RNA. However, it abolishes RNase H cleavage inside the modified wings, which is why gapmers keep a DNA central gap.

**Z-DNA biology, once dismissed as an artefact.**
- **ZBP1** senses Z-form nucleic acids through its Zα domains and triggers necroptosis.
- **ADAR1**'s Zα domain helps prevent self-RNA from activating innate immune sensors.
- ADAR1 Zα mutations cause Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, a neuroinflammatory encephalopathy relevant to paediatric neurology.
- Heat- and stress-induced Z-RNA is an active research area.

**Pitfalls in the lab.**
- Nearest-neighbour Tm predictions assume standard salt conditions. Mg2+ and dNTP concentrations shift actual melting.
- The A260/A280 ratio judges purity, not integrity.
- Crystal structures can distort groove widths through lattice contacts.

**Open questions.**
- How much do transient Hoogsteen states and minor-groove shape contribute to transcription factor specificity inside chromatin?
- Do quadruplexes and Z-forms work as genuine regulatory switches in vivo, or are they mostly by-products of supercoiling?
- Cryo-EM and in-cell NMR are now testing these ideas directly.

keyPoints: DNA is two antiparallel strands forming a right-handed double helix
A pairs with T (2 H-bonds), G pairs with C (3 H-bonds)
Base stacking, not hydrogen bonding, provides most helix stability
Unequal major and minor grooves let proteins read sequence without unwinding
B-DNA is the cellular form; A-form suits RNA duplexes; Z-DNA is left-handed
GC content and salt raise melting temperature (Tm)

lessons.title: DNA vs RNA: Chemical Differences and Roles

levels.kid:
Your cells keep two kinds of instruction molecules. One is **DNA**. The other is **RNA**.

Think of DNA as a giant, precious cookbook locked safely in the library. It is long, sturdy and has two strands twisted together, so it lasts a lifetime.

RNA is like a quick photocopy of one recipe. The copy is carried to the kitchen, where the cell's cooks build a protein. RNA usually has just one strand. It is made fast and thrown away fast, like a sticky note.

They also use slightly different letters. DNA uses A, T, C and G. RNA swaps T for a letter called **U**.

So DNA keeps the information safe, and RNA puts it to work.
levels.hs:
**DNA** (deoxyribonucleic acid) and **RNA** (ribonucleic acid) are both **nucleic acids**: chains of nucleotides joined by a sugar-phosphate backbone. But three chemical differences give them very different jobs.

- **Sugar:** DNA uses **deoxyribose**, which lacks an oxygen atom at the 2' ("two-prime") carbon. RNA uses **ribose**, which has a hydroxyl (-OH) group there. That extra -OH makes RNA more chemically reactive and easier to break.
- **Bases:** both use adenine (A), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). DNA uses **thymine (T)**; RNA uses **uracil (U)** instead. U pairs with A just like T does.
- **Strands:** DNA is usually a **double-stranded** helix. RNA is usually **single-stranded**, but it folds back on itself into hairpins and loops.

Because DNA is stable, it works as the long-term storage of genetic information. RNA is built for short-term action.

RNA comes in several types:
- **mRNA** (messenger RNA) carries a gene's message to the ribosome.
- **tRNA** (transfer RNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome.
- **rRNA** (ribosomal RNA) forms the core of the ribosome itself.

A real example: the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines used chemically modified mRNA. This works because mRNA is temporary. Cells read it, make a viral protein to train the immune system, then destroy it.
levels.college:
DNA and RNA share a backbone of nucleotides linked by **3'-5' phosphodiester bonds**, but small chemical changes produce large functional consequences.

**The 2'-hydroxyl.** Ribose carries a 2'-OH; deoxyribose does not. Under alkaline conditions or with metal ions, the 2'-OH can attack the neighbouring phosphorus. This cleaves the chain into a 2',3'-cyclic phosphate and a 5'-OH. This is why RNA is destroyed by alkali, while DNA survives. The 2'-OH also favours the **C3'-endo** sugar pucker, so RNA duplexes adopt an **A-form** helix rather than DNA's B-form.

**Thymine vs uracil.** Thymine is 5-methyluracil. Cytosine spontaneously **deaminates** to uracil. If DNA normally contained U, repair enzymes could not tell a damaged C from a genuine U. With T as the standard base, any U in DNA is flagged as damage and removed by **uracil-DNA glycosylase**. RNA is short-lived, so it can afford the cheaper base.

**Structure.** Double-stranded DNA keeps a backup copy of each sequence on the complementary strand, enabling repair. Single-stranded RNA folds into complex shapes:
- stems and hairpins
- non-canonical pairs such as **G-U wobble**
- tertiary contacts that bind ions and ligands

**Roles.**
- DNA: genome storage, faithful replication.
- mRNA: template for protein synthesis.
- tRNA and rRNA: decoding and peptide bond formation.
- Regulatory RNAs: **microRNAs**, long noncoding RNAs.
- Catalysis: **ribozymes**, RNAs with enzymatic activity.

**Turnover.** Bacterial mRNAs typically last minutes, and mammalian mRNAs last minutes to many hours. Short lifetimes let cells change protein output quickly. A DNA genome, by contrast, must persist for the life of the cell.
levels.phd:
The DNA/RNA division reflects a trade-off between **chemical versatility** and **informational stability**.

**Hydrolytic chemistry.** RNA self-cleavage proceeds by an in-line SN2-like attack of the 2'-oxygen on the adjacent phosphorus through a pentacoordinate transition state. Its rate depends on local geometry, since in-line alignment is required, and on general acid-base catalysis. Ribonucleases such as **RNase A** exploit this mechanism using His12 and His119. Uncatalysed, the phosphodiester bonds of DNA have half-lives estimated in the range of millions of years at neutral pH (Wolfenden). RNA linkages are many orders of magnitude more labile, with half-lives on the order of years and strongly sequence- and structure-dependent. In vivo, however, depurination and cytosine deamination of DNA, not backbone hydrolysis, dominate its spontaneous decay (Lindahl).

**Conformation.** The 2'-OH sterically and electronically favours C3'-endo pucker. A-form helices are short and wide, with a deep, narrow major groove and a shallow minor groove. RNA-DNA hybrids adopt intermediate geometries. These are recognized by **RNase H**, which matters for antisense oligonucleotide design.

**Thymine.** The C5 methyl group adds hydrophobic stacking and modestly stabilizes duplexes. Its main advantage is that deaminated cytosine can be detected and repaired. Thymidylate is made from dUMP by **thymidylate synthase** using a folate one-carbon donor, which makes it a major drug target (5-fluorouracil, methotrexate acting upstream via DHFR). Some bacteriophages, such as PBS1, carry uracil-containing DNA, which shows the rule is evolved, not obligatory.

**Deoxyribonucleotide synthesis.** All dNTPs come from NDPs via **ribonucleotide reductase**, a radical enzyme. This is consistent with the **RNA world** hypothesis: RNA came first, and DNA is a later chemical upgrade. Supporting evidence includes catalytic rRNA at the peptidyl transferase center (Ban, Nissen, Steitz, 2000), self-splicing introns (Cech) and RNase P (Altman), recognized by the 1989 Nobel Prize.

**Nuance.** The distinction is not absolute. RNA genomes exist in many viruses; DNA can form catalytic deoxyribozymes in vitro; and single-stranded DNA and double-stranded RNA both occur in nature.
levels.expert:
Practically, the DNA/RNA differences dictate how you handle samples, design drugs and interpret data.

**Bench pitfalls.**
- RNases are robust, often refold after boiling and are ubiquitous on skin. RNA work uses RNase inhibitors, guanidinium-based lysis (Chomczynski-Sacchi, TRIzol) and DEPC-treated or certified nuclease-free water.
- Genomic DNA contaminates RNA preps and inflates RT-qPCR signal. Use DNase treatment, no-RT controls and exon-junction-spanning primers.
- RNA integrity is scored as **RIN** (Agilent Bioanalyzer). Degraded clinical samples, such as FFPE tissue, bias toward 3' ends, which affects sequencing library choice.

**Therapeutic chemistry.** The 2'-position is the main handle for drug design. 2'-O-methyl, 2'-fluoro, 2'-O-methoxyethyl (MOE) and locked nucleic acid modifications raise nuclease resistance and binding affinity. They are used in siRNAs (e.g., GalNAc-conjugated drugs such as inclisiran) and antisense oligonucleotides. **Nusinersen**, a 2'-MOE antisense drug given intrathecally for spinal muscular atrophy, alters SMN2 splicing. Gapmer ASOs keep a central DNA window so RNase H can cleave the target RNA. **N1-methylpseudouridine** in mRNA vaccines (Karikó and Weissman, Nobel 2023) blunts innate sensing and increases translation.

**Immune discrimination.** Cells police location and chemistry. Cytosolic DNA triggers **cGAS-STING**, while uncapped 5'-triphosphate RNA activates RIG-I. Endosomal TLR7/8 sense single-stranded RNA and TLR9 senses unmethylated CpG DNA. Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, caused by mutations in genes including TREX1, RNASEH2 and ADAR1, is a neuroinflammatory disorder of failed nucleic-acid clearance or editing. It is relevant to pediatric neurology.

**Diagnostics.** Cerebrospinal fluid and plasma contain cell-free DNA and RNA. cfDNA "liquid biopsy" of CSF is being explored for glioma genotyping, for example IDH1 and H3 K27M variants. It may help where repeat brain biopsy is risky.

**Open questions.** These include how much of pervasive transcription is functional versus noise, and how RNA modifications (the epitranscriptome, e.g., m6A) govern neural plasticity. A further question is how to deliver oligonucleotides across the blood-brain barrier without intrathecal access.

keyPoints: DNA uses deoxyribose; RNA uses ribose with a 2'-OH group
The 2'-OH makes RNA more reactive and prone to cleavage, especially in alkali
DNA uses thymine; RNA uses uracil, which pairs with adenine
Thymine lets repair enzymes detect deaminated cytosine as damage
DNA is a stable double-stranded archive; RNA is mostly single-stranded and folds into shapes
RNA types include mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, regulatory RNAs and ribozymes

test.q: Which sugar is found in RNA?
test.explain: RNA contains ribose, which has a 2'-OH. Deoxyribose is the sugar in DNA.

test.q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
test.explain: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine. Cytosine and guanine are found in both.

test.q: Why is RNA less chemically stable than DNA?
test.explain: The 2'-OH can attack the neighbouring phosphodiester bond and cleave the backbone.

test.q: Which RNA type carries a gene's message to the ribosome?
test.explain: Messenger RNA is the template read by the ribosome. tRNA brings amino acids, and rRNA forms the ribosome.

test.q: What happens to RNA in alkaline conditions, compared with DNA?
test.explain: Alkali promotes 2'-OH attack, which cleaves RNA. DNA has no 2'-OH and survives.

test.q: What is the main advantage of DNA using thymine instead of uracil?
test.explain: Cytosine deaminates to uracil, so any U in DNA can be recognized as damage and repaired.

test.q: An RNA duplex usually adopts which helical form?
test.explain: The 2'-OH favours C3'-endo pucker, which produces the A-form helix.

test.q: RNA molecules that act as enzymes are called:
test.explain: Ribozymes are catalytic RNAs. Ribosomes are complexes of rRNA and protein, and their catalytic core is a ribozyme.

test.q: Why are mRNA vaccines able to be temporary in cells?
test.explain: mRNA is short-lived. Cells translate it, then destroy it.

test.q: In RNA, uracil pairs with ___.
test.explain: Uracil pairs with adenine, just as thymine does in DNA.

test.q: Name the DNA repair enzyme that removes uracil from DNA.
test.explain: Uracil-DNA glycosylase excises uracil arising from cytosine deamination.

test.q: The nucleotides of DNA and RNA are linked by 3'-5' ___ bonds.
test.explain: Phosphodiester bonds form the sugar-phosphate backbone of both nucleic acids.

kidTest.q: In the lesson, DNA is like what?
kidTest.explain: DNA is the safe, long-lasting cookbook of instructions.

kidTest.q: How many strands does RNA usually have?
kidTest.explain: RNA usually has one strand. DNA has two.

kidTest.q: What does an RNA copy help the cell build?
kidTest.explain: The RNA copy of a recipe is used to build a protein.

kidTest.q: Which molecule lasts a long time in the cell?
kidTest.explain: DNA is sturdy and lasts. RNA is made and thrown away fast.

kidTest.q: RNA uses the letter U in place of another DNA letter. What is that letter's full name? (Hint: t _ _ _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: DNA uses T, which stands for thymine; RNA swaps it for U.

advancedTest.q: An antisense gapmer keeps a central DNA window flanked by 2'-modified wings. What is the main purpose of the DNA window?
choices: To switch the hybrid into a Z-form helix
To let RNase H cleave the bound target RNA
To let reverse transcriptase copy the drug
To shield the duplex from most nucleases
advancedTest.explain: RNase H recognizes RNA-DNA hybrids. The modified wings add stability and affinity, but the DNA gap is needed for cleavage.

advancedTest.q: Ribonucleotide reductase makes every dNTP from ribonucleotides. Which hypothesis does this best support?
advancedTest.explain: Since deoxyribonucleotides are made from ribonucleotides, DNA looks like a later upgrade, which fits the RNA world hypothesis.

advancedTest.q: Uncatalysed DNA phosphodiester bonds are extremely stable. Which processes chiefly limit DNA integrity in vivo?
advancedTest.explain: Lindahl showed that base loss and deamination, not backbone hydrolysis, dominate spontaneous DNA decay. DNA has no 2'-OH.

advancedTest.q: Why does N1-methylpseudouridine improve mRNA vaccines?
choices: It converts the mRNA into stable DNA
It lets the mRNA replicate in cells
It adds a 2'-OH to stop translation
advancedTest.explain: This modified base reduces recognition by innate RNA sensors and increases translation. That is the Karikó-Weissman insight.

lessons.title: Chromatin: Histones and Nucleosomes

levels.kid:
Each of your cells holds about 2 meters of DNA. That is taller than a grown-up! But a cell is far too small to see. So how does all that DNA fit?

The cell winds DNA around tiny spools called **histones**. Think of thread wrapped around little beads. One bead with its thread is called a **nucleosome**. A long string of them looks like beads on a necklace.

The necklace then coils and folds again and again, like a phone cord twisting up. This packed DNA is called **chromatin**.

There is a clever trick, too. Tightly packed parts are hard for the cell to read. Loose parts are easy to read. So packing also helps decide which genes get used.
levels.hs:
Human cells contain roughly 2 meters of DNA, yet the nucleus is only about 6 micrometers across. Cells solve this packing problem with **chromatin**: DNA combined with proteins.

The main packing proteins are **histones**. They are small and positively charged because they are rich in the amino acids **lysine** and **arginine**. That positive charge attracts DNA's negatively charged phosphate backbone.

The basic packing unit is the **nucleosome**:
- Eight histone proteins form a core called the **histone octamer**. It contains two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
- About 147 base pairs of DNA wrap around this core about 1.7 times.
- Short stretches of **linker DNA** connect one nucleosome to the next. A fifth histone, **H1**, sits where DNA enters and leaves the core.

Under an electron microscope, unfolded chromatin looks like "beads on a string." The nucleosomes then fold into more compact structures, and in a dividing cell the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes.

Chromatin comes in two broad states. **Euchromatin** is loosely packed, and its genes are usually active. **Heterochromatin** is tightly packed, and its genes are usually silent. One example of heterochromatin is the DNA around centromeres. Packing therefore controls gene activity as well as storage.
levels.college:
Chromatin is the DNA-protein complex of eukaryotic nuclei. By mass it is roughly half DNA and half protein, mostly histones.

**Core histones.** H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 share a **histone fold**, which is three alpha-helices joined by two loops. Pairs of histones dimerize in a "handshake" arrangement:
- An (H3-H4)₂ tetramer is deposited first.
- Two H2A-H2B dimers then join to complete the octamer.
- About 147 bp of DNA wrap in roughly 1.65 left-handed superhelical turns.
- Arginine side chains insert into the DNA's minor groove wherever it faces the octamer.
- Contacts are mainly with the sugar-phosphate backbone, so histones bind largely independently of sequence. Sequences that bend easily are still favored.

**Histone tails.** Flexible N-terminal tails extend out from the core. Their lysines and arginines carry **post-translational modifications**:
- **Acetylation** by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) neutralizes lysine's positive charge, loosening chromatin. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) reverse it.
- **Methylation** can activate or repress depending on the site. H3K4me3 marks active promoters, while H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 mark silenced regions.
- **Phosphorylation** of H3S10 accompanies mitotic condensation.

**Linker histone H1** binds the nucleosome dyad and linker DNA, forming the **chromatosome** (about 167 bp). H1 promotes compaction.

**Histone variants** replace canonical histones at specific sites:
- **H2A.Z** sits at promoters.
- **CENP-A**, an H3 variant, marks centromeres.
- **H3.3** is deposited in active genes independently of replication.
- **H2A.X** is phosphorylated (γH2AX) at DNA breaks.

**Higher order.** The 10-nm beads-on-a-string fiber was long thought to fold into a regular **30-nm fiber**. Current views of that fiber are covered under advanced levels. Mitotic chromosomes show the most extreme compaction.
levels.phd:
The 2.8 Å crystal structure of the nucleosome core particle (Luger, Richmond and colleagues, 1997; refined to 1.9 Å in 2002) defined its architecture. The DNA wraps in 1.65 left-handed turns, giving negative supercoiling that is constrained by the protein rather than free in the DNA. At 14 sites, spaced one helical turn apart, the minor groove faces the octamer. Each site contributes several hydrogen bonds and arginine insertions, totaling roughly 120 direct contacts. The dyad axis passes through superhelical location 0, where the H3-H4 tetramer engages the central DNA.

Kornberg proposed the nucleosome in 1974. His proposal combined nuclease digestion ladders with Olins and Olins' "ν bodies" seen by electron microscopy. Micrococcal nuclease cuts linker DNA preferentially, which yields multiples of around 200 bp. This principle underlies MNase-seq today.

**Positioning.** Nucleosomes favor sequences in which AA/TT/TA dinucleotides recur about every 10 bp where the minor groove faces inward. Poly(dA:dT) tracts resist bending and help form nucleosome-depleted regions at promoters. Genome-wide, however, positions depend heavily on ATP-dependent remodelers and on barriers such as transcription factors. The relative weight of these factors versus intrinsic sequence was debated (Segal 2006 vs Zhang 2009).

**Dynamics.** Polach and Widom described **site exposure**: DNA transiently unwraps from the octamer ends. This "breathing" gives factors access on millisecond timescales, with equilibrium constants of roughly 10⁻² to 10⁻⁵ depending on depth into the wrap.

**Remodelers.** Four families of SF2 ATPases translocate DNA across the octamer:
- SWI/SNF, which slides or ejects nucleosomes.
- ISWI, which spaces nucleosomes evenly.
- CHD, which also spaces and assembles nucleosomes.
- INO80/SWR1, which exchanges H2A.Z.

**The 30-nm controversy.** The solenoid model (Finch and Klug) and the zigzag model came from studies of reconstituted fibers under specific salt conditions. Cryo-electron microscopy of vitrified sections and ChromEMT (Ou et al., 2017) instead showed irregular 5-24 nm chains with variable density in interphase nuclei. Single-molecule methods and Hi-C support **polymer-melt** or liquid-like packing over a regular hierarchy. The 2014 cryo-EM structure of a 30-nm fiber (Song et al.) may describe local tetranucleosome motifs rather than long fibers in vivo.
levels.expert:
Several frontiers now extend nucleosome biology into the clinic and into new methods.

**Oncohistones.** Lysine-to-methionine mutations act dominantly even though histone genes are multicopy:
- **H3K27M** occurs in diffuse midline glioma, formerly DIPG, a neurosurgically unresectable pediatric tumor. The mutant tail occupies the active site of PRC2 subunit EZH2. This inhibits PRC2 and causes global loss of H3K27me3, even though only a few percent of H3 is mutant.
- **H3G34R/V** drives hemispheric pediatric high-grade glioma.
- **H3K36M** drives chondroblastoma.

The WHO CNS5 classification (2021) defines "diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered." Biopsy for the molecular diagnosis is now routine, typically with stereotactic sampling. The imipridone ONC201 (dordaviprone), a DRD2 antagonist and ClpP agonist, showed responses in H3K27M glioma and received accelerated FDA approval in 2025.

**Epigenetic drugs.** HDAC inhibitors (vorinostat, romidepsin) are approved for T-cell lymphomas, and the EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat for epithelioid sarcoma. Their effects are pleiotropic because HDACs also deacetylate non-histone proteins such as p53 and tubulin. Calling them simply "chromatin openers" is therefore an oversimplification.

**Measuring chromatin.** Each assay has blind spots:
- **ATAC-seq** uses Tn5 to tag accessible DNA. It reports accessibility, not activity.
- **CUT&RUN** and **CUT&Tag** have largely replaced ChIP-seq for low-input samples.
- **MNase-seq** results depend on digestion extent. Fragile nucleosomes, such as H2A.Z/H3.3 particles, disappear under heavy digestion, which created artifactual "nucleosome-free" regions.
- **Hi-C** and **Micro-C** resolve loops down to the nucleosome level.

**Mechanistic advances.** Cryo-EM has captured remodelers, Pol II transcribing through nucleosomes, and pioneer factors such as Sox2 and OCT4 binding partially unwrapped DNA. These structures show how such factors open closed chromatin. Phase separation driven by HP1 and linker-histone condensates is proposed as a mechanism of heterochromatin compaction. Its in vivo relevance is still contested, because some "condensates" may reflect overexpression artifacts.

**Open questions.** Is the "histone code" causal or merely correlative? Yeast studies mutating H3K4 and other residues found surprisingly mild transcriptional effects. Other unresolved questions are how marks are inherited through replication when parental histones are split between daughter strands, and how nucleosome mechanics shape mutation rates.

keyPoints: Chromatin is DNA plus proteins, mainly histones, packed into the nucleus
A nucleosome is about 147 bp of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer (2 each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4)
Histones are rich in lysine and arginine, so they attract DNA's negative backbone
Linker histone H1 binds linker DNA and promotes compaction
Tail modifications such as acetylation and methylation regulate access to genes
Euchromatin is open and active; heterochromatin is compact and usually silent

test.q: Which proteins form the nucleosome core octamer?
choices: Four each of H3 and H4 alone
Two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4
Two each of H1, H2B, H3 and H4
Two each of H1, H2A, H3 and H4
test.explain: The core octamer contains two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. H1 is the linker histone outside the core.

test.q: Why do histones bind DNA so tightly?
choices: They pair with the bases by hydrogen bonds
They form covalent links to the deoxyribose
Their negative residues attract the bases
Their positive residues attract the phosphates
test.explain: Lysine and arginine are positively charged, and they attract DNA's negatively charged phosphate backbone.

test.q: Roughly how much DNA wraps around one nucleosome core?
test.explain: About 147 bp wraps the octamer roughly 1.65-1.7 times.

test.q: Histone acetylation generally does what to chromatin?
choices: Cuts it at the linker DNA regions
Loosens it by neutralizing lysine charge
Condenses it by adding positive charge
test.explain: Acetylation removes lysine's positive charge, which weakens histone-DNA attraction and opens chromatin.

test.q: Which enzymes remove acetyl groups from histones?
test.explain: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove acetyl groups. HATs are the enzymes that add them.

test.q: Heterochromatin is best described as:
test.explain: Heterochromatin is compact and its genes are typically silent. Euchromatin is the open, active form.

test.q: Which histone variant marks centromeres?
test.explain: CENP-A is the H3 variant found at centromeres. H2A.Z marks promoters and H2A.X marks DNA breaks.

test.q: The 'beads-on-a-string' appearance corresponds to:
test.explain: Nucleosomes (beads) joined by linker DNA (string) form the 10-nm fiber.

test.q: Which mark is associated with active promoters?
test.explain: H3K4me3 marks active promoters. H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 are repressive, and H3S10 phosphorylation accompanies mitosis.

test.q: Which linker histone binds where DNA enters and exits the nucleosome?
test.explain: H1 binds the dyad and the linker DNA, forming the chromatosome.

test.q: The DNA connecting one nucleosome to the next is called ___ DNA.
test.explain: Linker DNA joins adjacent nucleosomes and is preferentially cut by micrococcal nuclease.

test.q: Loosely packed, usually active chromatin is called ___.
test.explain: Euchromatin is open and transcriptionally active.

kidTest.q: What does DNA wrap around in a cell?
kidTest.explain: DNA winds around histone proteins like thread on a spool.

kidTest.q: How much DNA is in one of your cells?
kidTest.explain: About 2 meters of DNA is packed into each cell.

kidTest.q: A string of nucleosomes looks like what?
kidTest.explain: The spools along the DNA look like beads on a string.

kidTest.q: Which DNA is easiest for the cell to read?
kidTest.explain: Loose parts are easy for the cell to read.

kidTest.q: Packed DNA with its proteins is called c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Chromatin is DNA plus the proteins that pack it.

advancedTest.q: H3K27M mutates only a few percent of H3 yet causes global loss of H3K27me3. The best explanation is:
choices: The mutant tail directly demethylates nearby wild-type histones
The mutant tail inhibits PRC2 by occupying the EZH2 active site
The mutation silences the remaining wild-type H3 genes
Methionine blocks nucleosome assembly across the genome
advancedTest.explain: K27M binds the EZH2 active site and inhibits PRC2 catalytically, which explains its dominant effect despite low abundance.

advancedTest.q: Why did cryo-EM of vitrified nuclei challenge the 30-nm fiber model?
choices: It found no nucleosomes in interphase nuclei
It found 30-nm fibers restricted to heterochromatin
It showed irregular 5-24 nm chains rather than regular fibers
It showed DNA wrapped right-handed around octamers
advancedTest.explain: In situ imaging such as ChromEMT revealed disordered chains. The 30-nm fiber appeared mainly in reconstituted fibers under specific salt conditions.

advancedTest.q: Heavy MNase digestion makes a promoter appear nucleosome-free. A cautious interpretation is:
choices: Fragile H2A.Z/H3.3 nucleosomes may have been digested away
Linker histone H1 resists digestion at promoters
The promoter lacks nucleosomes in living cells
Tn5 tagging has created a false gap
advancedTest.explain: MNase results depend on digestion extent. Fragile variant nucleosomes can vanish under heavy digestion, creating artifactual gaps.

advancedTest.q: How can a transcription factor bind a site buried inside a nucleosome without a remodeler?
choices: By replacing H3 with CENP-A at that site
Through site exposure as DNA transiently unwraps
By cutting the linker DNA to free the site
By acetylating the DNA bases directly
advancedTest.explain: Polach and Widom showed that DNA breathes off the octamer ends, briefly exposing sites with an equilibrium that depends on depth into the wrap.

lessons.title: The Central Dogma and Its Exceptions

levels.kid:
Your body follows a recipe book called **DNA**. It is kept safe inside each cell, like a precious cookbook that never leaves the library.

When the cell needs something, it copies one recipe onto a little note called **RNA**. The note travels out to the cell's kitchen. There, tiny machines read the note and build a **protein**. Proteins do the work, like building muscles or carrying air in your blood.

So the path goes: DNA, then RNA, then protein. Scientists call this the **central dogma**.

But nature has surprises! Some viruses can turn RNA back into DNA. And some RNA notes never become proteins at all. They do jobs all by themselves.
levels.hs:
The **central dogma of molecular biology** describes how genetic information flows in cells. Francis Crick proposed it in 1958:

- **Replication**: DNA is copied to make more DNA before a cell divides.
- **Transcription**: a gene's DNA sequence is copied into **messenger RNA (mRNA)**.
- **Translation**: ribosomes read the mRNA three letters at a time (a **codon**) and join amino acids into a protein.

The key idea is direction. Information can move from nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) to protein. It never moves from protein back to nucleic acid. A protein's amino acid sequence cannot be used to rewrite a gene.

There are important exceptions to the simple "DNA to RNA to protein" picture:
- **Reverse transcription**: HIV, a **retrovirus**, carries RNA and uses an enzyme called **reverse transcriptase** to make DNA from it. That DNA is inserted into the host's chromosomes.
- **RNA replication**: viruses such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2 copy RNA directly into RNA.
- **Non-coding RNA**: many RNAs, like ribosomal RNA and transfer RNA, are never translated. They are the finished product.

Pharmacology connection: drugs like zidovudine (AZT) block reverse transcriptase. That attacks a step that human cells do not normally rely on.
levels.college:
Crick stated the **sequence hypothesis** and the **central dogma** in 1958 and clarified them in a 1970 *Nature* paper. The dogma is often misquoted as "DNA makes RNA makes protein." Crick's actual claim was narrower: once sequence information has passed into protein, it cannot get out again.

Crick grouped the transfers:
- **General transfers** (occur in all cells): DNA→DNA (replication), DNA→RNA (transcription), RNA→protein (translation).
- **Special transfers** (only in some situations): RNA→RNA (RNA-dependent RNA polymerases of RNA viruses), RNA→DNA (reverse transcription), and DNA→protein directly. The last has been shown only in cell-free experiments, using ribosomes with antibiotics such as neomycin.
- **Unknown transfers** (proposed never to occur): protein→protein, protein→DNA and protein→RNA.

**Reverse transcriptase** was discovered independently by Howard Temin and David Baltimore in 1970, earning a Nobel Prize in 1975. It is not just a viral oddity:
- **Telomerase** is a ribonucleoprotein that reverse-transcribes its own RNA template to extend chromosome ends.
- **LINE-1 retrotransposons** encode a reverse transcriptase. Retroelements make up roughly 40% of the human genome.

Other complications for the simple linear model:
- Most of the genome is transcribed into **non-coding RNAs** (rRNA, tRNA, snRNA, miRNA, lncRNA) that function without being translated.
- **RNA editing** (A-to-I by ADAR enzymes, C-to-U by APOBEC1) changes the sequence after transcription, so the protein can differ from the genomic code.
- **Alternative splicing** lets one gene produce many protein isoforms.

None of these break Crick's core rule, because information still does not flow back out of protein.
levels.phd:
Crick's 1958 "On Protein Synthesis" lecture laid out two ideas. The sequence hypothesis says nucleic acid sequence specifies amino acid sequence. The central dogma is a negative statement about which residue-by-residue transfers of sequence are possible. In his 1970 reply to the "Central Dogma Reversed" editorial (written after Temin and Baltimore's reports), Crick stressed that reverse transcription was allowed under his framework all along. What he had forbidden was a mechanism to back-translate protein. No such process is plausible: it would need sequence-specific reading of polypeptides and a reverse genetic code, and the code's degeneracy (61 sense codons for 20 amino acids) makes the inverse many-to-one problem underdetermined.

**Prions** are the case most often called a violation. In PrP^Sc templating, a misfolded conformer catalyzes the refolding of native PrP^C, and yeast [PSI+] (Sup35) shows this can be heritable. Yet what spreads is conformation, not sequence. The polypeptide sequence is still encoded by the PRNP gene, so prions show protein-based inheritance of a phenotype rather than sequence transfer out of protein. That is why prions are better described as an epigenetic challenge than a formal exception.

The Baltimore classification (seven classes) of viruses is in effect a map of how each viral genome reaches mRNA. Class VI retroviruses go RNA→DNA→RNA. Class VII hepadnaviruses (hepatitis B) go DNA→RNA→DNA through a pregenomic RNA. Negative-sense RNA viruses must package their own RdRp, because a host cell cannot copy RNA from RNA.

Endogenous reverse transcription shapes eukaryotic genomes. L1 ORF2p carries out target-primed reverse transcription, producing processed pseudogenes and retrogenes that lack introns. The TERT catalytic subunit of telomerase is phylogenetically related to retroelement reverse transcriptases.

Modern nuance concerns the linear view. RNA editing, recoding (selenocysteine at UGA, programmed ribosomal frameshifting) and the ribozyme activity of the ribosome itself (the peptidyl transferase center is rRNA) all fit the **RNA world** hypothesis, in which RNA was once both genome and catalyst. This suggests DNA and protein are later specializations.
levels.expert:
For a clinician-scientist, the special transfers in Crick's scheme are drug targets. Host cells normally lack RNA-dependent polymerases of their own (endogenous reverse transcriptases aside), so viral polymerases offer selective chokepoints:
- **Nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors** (tenofovir, emtricitabine) act as chain terminators because they lack a 3'-OH. **Non-nucleoside RTIs** (efavirenz, rilpivirine) bind an allosteric pocket. **Integrase inhibitors** (dolutegravir) block the integration step that follows reverse transcription.
- **RdRp inhibitors**: sofosbuvir (an NS5B nucleotide analog) transformed hepatitis C into a curable infection. Remdesivir causes delayed chain termination in SARS-CoV-2 RdRp. Molnupiravir works by lethal mutagenesis, pushing error rates past the viral error threshold.
- Hepatitis B persists as nuclear **cccDNA**, which polymerase inhibitors do not eliminate. This is the main obstacle to a functional cure.

Pitfalls: mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ toxicity from older NRTIs, and the rapid evolution of resistance in error-prone polymerases, which drives combination therapy.

RNA medicine runs along the dogma deliberately. mRNA vaccines deliver modified mRNA (N1-methylpseudouridine, the work of Karikó and Weissman, Nobel Prize 2023) straight to the translation step. Antisense oligonucleotides (nusinersen modulating SMN2 splicing) and siRNAs (patisiran) act at the RNA level without touching DNA. Prime editing borrows reverse transcription itself: a Cas9 nickase is fused to an engineered M-MLV reverse transcriptase that writes an edit from a pegRNA template.

Neurologically relevant extensions:
- Prion diseases (CJD, fatal familial insomnia) remain untreatable. PRNP-lowering antisense oligonucleotides are in trials, a sequence-level attack on a conformational disease.
- Somatic L1 retrotransposition in neurons has been reported, but its frequency is debated. Estimates differ by orders of magnitude depending on single-cell sequencing artifacts.
- Activity-regulated Arc protein forms capsid-like particles that carry RNA between neurons. It is a domesticated retrotransposon gene.

An open question is how often reverse transcription contributes to somatic mosaicism and disease, for example in reports of APP gene recombination in Alzheimer's disease.

keyPoints: Central dogma: sequence information flows DNA to RNA to protein, never back out of protein
Replication, transcription and translation are the general transfers
Reverse transcriptase (Temin and Baltimore, 1970) makes DNA from RNA
RNA viruses copy RNA to RNA with an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Many RNAs (rRNA, tRNA, miRNA) function without being translated
Prions spread a protein shape, not sequence information

test.q: Which process copies a gene's DNA sequence into mRNA?
test.explain: Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template. Translation is the next step, where mRNA is read to build a protein.

test.q: According to Crick, which transfer of sequence information is forbidden?
test.explain: Crick's core rule is that sequence information does not flow out of protein, so protein to RNA is forbidden. DNA replication is a general transfer. RNA replication and RNA to DNA (reverse transcription) are allowed as special transfers.

test.q: Which enzyme lets HIV make DNA from its RNA genome?
test.explain: Reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA, which is then integrated into the host genome.

test.q: Who independently discovered reverse transcriptase in 1970?
test.explain: Howard Temin and David Baltimore shared the 1975 Nobel Prize for this discovery.

test.q: Which human enzyme uses reverse transcription to extend chromosome ends?
test.explain: Telomerase reverse-transcribes its own RNA template to add telomere repeats.

test.q: Which RNA functions without being translated into protein?
test.explain: tRNA is a finished non-coding product. mRNA and pre-mRNA carry coding information meant for translation.

test.q: Why are prions usually not counted as a true exception to the dogma?
choices: They copy a shape, not a sequence
They are made of RNA, not protein
test.explain: Misfolded PrP templates the folding of normal PrP, but its sequence still comes from the PRNP gene.

test.q: RNA editing by ADAR enzymes means that:
choices: DNA is rebuilt using protein as a template
Introns are inserted into the mature mRNA
Protein can differ from the gene's code
Ribosomes skip over the normal start codon
test.explain: A-to-I editing changes the RNA sequence after transcription, so the protein can differ from what the gene encodes.

test.q: Viruses like influenza copy their genome using:
test.explain: RNA viruses carry an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) to make RNA from RNA, because host cells cannot do this.

test.q: Which scientist proposed the central dogma in 1958?
test.explain: Francis Crick stated it in his 1958 lecture and clarified it in 1970.

test.q: Ribosomes read mRNA in three-letter units called ___.
test.explain: Each codon specifies one amino acid or a stop signal.

test.q: What is the general name for a virus like HIV that reverse-transcribes its RNA genome?
test.explain: Retroviruses convert their RNA into DNA and insert it into host chromosomes.

kidTest.q: What is the usual order in the central dogma?
kidTest.explain: The recipe (DNA) is copied to a note (RNA), which is used to build protein.

kidTest.q: What does the RNA note do?
choices: It carries a recipe to the kitchen
kidTest.explain: RNA carries a copy of a recipe out to where proteins are made.

kidTest.q: What do proteins do?
choices: They hold the main recipe book
They do work like carrying air
kidTest.explain: Proteins are the workers, building muscle and carrying oxygen.

kidTest.q: What surprise can some viruses do?
kidTest.explain: Some viruses, like HIV, can make DNA from RNA.

kidTest.q: The cell's recipe book is called D _ _.
kidTest.explain: DNA holds the recipes for making proteins.

advancedTest.q: Why is back-translation from protein to nucleic acid considered implausible, beyond simply never having been observed?
choices: Proteins lack the nitrogen needed to make new bases
Ribosomes degrade proteins soon after making them
Reverse transcriptase uses up the available nucleotides
Code degeneracy makes the inverse mapping underdetermined
advancedTest.explain: With 61 sense codons for 20 amino acids, a protein sequence does not specify a unique nucleic acid sequence. It would also need a sequence-reading machine that does not exist.

advancedTest.q: A negative-sense RNA virus must package its own RdRp in the virion mainly because:
choices: Host reverse transcriptase would convert it to DNA
Its genome is unstable without an attached protein
Host cells lack enzymes to copy RNA from RNA
advancedTest.explain: The negative-sense genome cannot be translated directly, and the host has no RdRp to make mRNA from it, so the virus must bring the enzyme along.

advancedTest.q: Polymerase inhibitors suppress hepatitis B but rarely cure it, because:
choices: Nuclear cccDNA persists outside the polymerase step
Its RdRp is fully resistant to nucleoside analogs
The virus lacks a reverse transcription step in its cycle
It integrates as a provirus by its own integrase
advancedTest.explain: HBV (a class VII virus) keeps a stable cccDNA reservoir in the nucleus that blocking reverse transcription does not remove.

advancedTest.q: Processed pseudogenes in the human genome lack introns. This best indicates that they arose from:
choices: L1-mediated reverse transcription of spliced mRNA
Direct translation of DNA without RNA
Unequal crossing over between two sister chromatids
advancedTest.explain: Introns are removed by splicing at the mRNA stage. A gene copy lacking introns points to an mRNA that was reverse-transcribed (by L1 ORF2p) and reinserted into the genome.
